content: 1. Disease surveillance systems for communicable diseases should be implemented nationwide, while hepatitis programs can be established at sentinel sites. 2. Hepatitis programs should coordinate with other stakeholders to conduct biomarker surveys effectively. 3. Vital registration systems should be utilized to track hepatitis-related deaths. 4. Sentinel sites should focus on managing patients with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 5. Cancer registries should be used to monitor cases of HCC and other liver-related malignancies. 6. Case definitions for hepatitis surveillance should include presumptive and confirmed cases of acute hepatitis, chronic HBV and HCV infections, and serological evidence of past or present HCV infection. 7. Surveillance activities aim to detect outbreaks, describe trends in type-specific acute hepatitis, identify risk factors, estimate infection prevalence, model incidence trends, and estimate mortality from HBVor HCV-associated HCC and cirrhosis. 8. In-vitro diagnostic testing should be organized during outbreaks, focusing on reliable diagnostics and risk factor data from tertiary centers rather than low-quality data from multiple sites. 9. Surveillance for acute hepatitis cannot directly quantify new infections due to underreporting and the high proportion of asymptomatic cases. Adjustments are necessary to account for these factors. 10. WHO surveillance case definitions for viral hepatitis are designed for reporting and may differ from clinical management criteria. 11. Biomarker and epidemiological criteria are essential for confirming cases of acute hepatitis, including specific serological markers like IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HEV, IgM anti-HBc, and HCV RNA. 12. Chronic infections require biomarker confirmation, such as HBsAg positivity for HBV or HCV RNA positivity for HCV. 13. Syndromic surveillance, based on clinical features, is a baseline standard for detecting large outbreaks, particularly of hepatitis A and E, but is limited in its ability to capture detailed data. 14. Enhanced case reporting, using clinical and biomarker criteria, is more informative and can be implemented at sentinel sites with access to diagnostic testing and trained staff. 15. Enhanced case reporting allows for the identification of trends in type-specific acute hepatitis and helps generate hypotheses about transmission modes, such as injection drug use or unsafe healthcare practices. 16. Biomarker surveys are the gold standard for estimating the prevalence of chronic infections and guiding testing and treatment strategies. 17. Biomarker surveys should be integrated with other health-related population surveys to optimize resources and provide comprehensive data. 18. Testing stored sera may raise methodological and ethical issues, including lack of participant consent for additional testing and inability to link identified cases to care. 19. Reporting cases of chronic infection presenting to healthcare facilities helps monitor testing, treatment, and care services but cannot estimate prevalence. 20. Surveillance among high-risk groups, such as people who inject drugs and prisoners, provides critical data on risk behaviors and infection prevalence. 21. Estimating the fraction of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to HBV and HCV infections is essential for evaluating the impact of hepatitis elimination efforts. 22. Vital registration systems should record hepatitis-associated deaths under categories like acute hepatitis, cirrhosis, or HCC, with attributable fractions estimated for specific causes. 23. Data abstraction from clinical records at sentinel sites or cancer registries can help estimate the attributable fraction of sequelae to viral hepatitis. 24. WHO’s Global Reporting System for Hepatitis enables countries to report the fraction of cirrhosis and HCC attributable to HBV and HCV. 25. Monitoring and evaluation frameworks for viral hepatitis should include core indicators reflecting the cascade of care for HBV and cure for HCV. 26. Measuring the prevalence of HBV infection among children under five years, defined by HBsAg presence, serves as a surrogate indicator for the cumulative incidence of chronic HBV infections. 27. Data systems for hepatitis surveillance should include acute hepatitis surveillance, biomarker surveys, and monitoring of testing and treatment cascades. 28. Aggregate data reporting from healthcare facilities involved in treatment is less resource-intensive and suitable for early-stage programs. 29. Individual patient databases can provide longitudinal data but require significant resources for data entry and management. 30. Automated data analysis can aggregate individual data and calculate core indicators for diagnosis, treatment, and effectiveness, facilitating national and global reporting. 31. Surveillance systems should prioritize high-prevalence groups for focused testing and monitoring, such as people who inject drugs and prisoners. 32. Integration of hepatitis surveillance with other health programs, such as HIV or tuberculosis, can enhance efficiency and resource utilization. 33. WHO provides template protocols for biomarker surveys, enhanced case reporting, and surveillance of sequelae to guide countries in implementing effective hepatitis surveillance systems. 34. Monitoring the cascade of testing and treatment improves patient management and identifies bottlenecks in care continuity. 35. National health information systems should coordinate data collection and reporting to ensure comprehensive monitoring and evaluation of hepatitis programs. 36. Electronic medical records and reporting systems can streamline data management and support the cascade of care from individual patient monitoring to aggregate reporting. 37. Surveillance data should be used to inform public health strategies, guide resource allocation, and evaluate the impact of hepatitis elimination efforts.
